title: 想在家用 PC 集群上运行大规模 AI 模型吗？
author: Ian Cowley
content:
If you've tried running models like Qwen2-57B or Mixtral-8x22B (141B parameters) locally, you've probably hit the hard physical ceiling of consumer hardware: VRAM exhaustion.

A single consumer GPU tops out around 8GB, 12GB, or 16GB of VRAM. Squeezing a 141B Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model into one box usually demands an enterprise-grade 80GB datacenter accelerator costing thousands.

Meanwhile, look around your desk or home lab:

  • A workstation with an RTX 3060 (12GB)
  • A laptop with an RTX 4060 (8GB)
  • A mini PC with an AMD Radeon 680M/780M iGPU sharing DDR5 system memory
  • A secondary machine with an AVX-512 capable CPU running Linux

What if you could turn that collection of mismatched, heterogeneous hardware into a single pipeline cluster over a standard home gigabit network?

That is why I built Glacier.Inference.Distributed.

The Core Idea: Heterogeneous Pipeline Parallelism

Instead of requiring uniform cluster hardware or complex distributed training frameworks, Glacier.Inference.Distributed partitions GGUF transformer models across $N$ machines using pipeline parallelism.

Model layers are sliced across available nodes. A single token's hidden state activation flows sequentially across the cluster: 

[Token IDs]
     │
     ▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Node 0: Host Laptop (RTX 4060)               │
│ Embeddings + Root Attention Blocks 0..N1     │
└──────────────────────┬───────────────────────┘
                       │ Fused Wire Frame (INT8 / FP16)
                       ▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Node 1: Desktop (RTX 3060 12GB)              │
│ Transformer Blocks N1+1..N2                  │
└──────────────────────┬───────────────────────┘
                       │ Streaming Socket Frame
                       ▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Node 2: Mini PC (AMD Radeon 680M APU)        │
│ Transformer Blocks N2+1..N3                  │
└──────────────────────┬───────────────────────┘
                       │ Low-Latency Socket Frame
                       ▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Node 3: Linux Server (Ryzen Zen 5 AVX-512)   │
│ Final Blocks N3+1..End + LM Head / Logits    │
└──────────────────────┬───────────────────────┘
                       │ Next Token ID
                       ▼
                  [Next Token]

Isn't LAN Latency the Bottleneck?

The most common assumption with distributed inference is that standard 1000BASE-T Gigabit Ethernet will choke the token generation speed.

In practice, the math proves otherwise.

During the sequential decode phase of an LLM, the cluster does not exchange model weights over the wire—each node keeps its assigned layers resident in local VRAM or system RAM. The only data crossing the network per token is the activation tensor (the hidden state vector).

For a model with hidden dimension $d = 3584$:

  • In FP32, that is $14.3 \text{ KB}$ per token.
  • Quantized dynamically to symmetric INT8 over the wire, it is just $5.1 \text{ KB}$ per hop.

Over standard Gigabit Ethernet:

  • One LAN hop takes roughly 0.45 ms.
  • A full 3-hop traversal takes ~7.88 ms.

When running heavy models, computing the multi-head attention and MoE feed-forward networks across active parameters takes hundreds of milliseconds to seconds. A ~8 ms wire delay accounts for less than 0.2% of total token execution time, leaving 99.8% of the run spent on raw compute.

Zero Dependencies: 100% Pure C# .NET 10

Most distributed AI stacks drag along dozens of heavy dependencies: CUDA toolkit installations, Python runtime environments, Torch binaries, and native C++ orchestration wrappers.

Glacier.Inference.Distributed is built from the metal up in pure C# targeting .NET 10 (and is Native AOT-ready):

  • Zero Python. Zero C++ dependencies.
  • Network Pipeline: Built with System.IO.Pipelines utilizing 64-byte aligned socket framing (ClusterFrameHeader + FusedActivationHeader).
  • Memory Invariant: 0 Gen 0, Gen 1, or Gen 2 garbage collections and 0 bytes of managed heap allocations during the hot decode loop.
  • Hardware Acceleration: Automatically routes computation to discrete GPUs (via Direct3D 12), integrated APUs, or multithreaded SIMD / AVX-512 vector paths on CPUs.

Slicing Real Models: Sizing Reference

Because the coordinator auto-inspects standard GGUF metadata, it automatically calculates layer boundaries and hidden dimensions based on the nodes you provide:

Model Architecture Parameters Active per Token Slicing Example (4 Nodes) Disk Footprint
Qwen2-57B-A14B 57B 14B (8/64 MoE) 7 layers / node (28 total) ~25.6 GB (Q3_K_M)
Mixtral-8x22B 141B 39B (2/8 MoE) 14 layers / node (56 total) ~35.3 GB (IQ2_XXS)
Mixtral-8x7B 47B 13B (2/8 MoE) 8 layers / node (32 total) ~26.4 GB (Q4_K_M)
DeepSeek-R1-Distill-14B 14.7B 14.7B (Dense) 12 layers / node (48 total) ~9.0 GB (Q4_K_M)

Hands-On: Setting Up a 4-Node Home Cluster

1. Clone on All Nodes

Install the .NET 10 SDK on your machines and clone the repo: 

git clone https://github.com/ian-cowley/Glacier.Inference.Distributed.git
cd Glacier.Inference.Distributed

2. Download the Model

Rather than using huggingface-cli or external Python tools, Glacier includes a pure C# multi-stream HTTP Range downloader that opens concurrent sockets to saturate your bandwidth: 

# Download Qwen2-57B
dotnet run --project src/Glacier.Inference.Distributed.Cli -c Release -- download qwen2-57b

# Or download Mixtral-8x22B (141B)
dotnet run --project src/Glacier.Inference.Distributed.Cli -c Release -- download mixtral-8x22b

3. Spin Up Worker Daemons

On your secondary machines, start the worker daemon. Each worker auto-detects whether to initialize D3D12 GPU shaders or CPU SIMD: 

# On Machine 1 (e.g. 192.168.1.108 with RTX 3060):
dotnet run --project src/Glacier.Inference.Distributed.Cli -c Release -- --role worker --port 5055

# On Machine 2 (e.g. 192.168.1.101 with Radeon 680M):
dotnet run --project src/Glacier.Inference.Distributed.Cli -c Release -- --role worker --port 5056

# On Machine 3 (e.g. 192.168.1.200 Linux CPU box):
dotnet run --project src/Glacier.Inference.Distributed.Cli -c Release -- --role worker --port 5057

4. Fire Up the Coordinator

From your primary machine (e.g., host laptop), point the coordinator to the worker endpoints: 

dotnet run --project src/Glacier.Inference.Distributed.Cli -c Release -- \
  --role coordinator \
  --stages 192.168.1.108:5055,192.168.1.101:5056,192.168.1.200:5057 \
  --model ./models/qwen2-57b-a14b-instruct-q3_k_m.gguf \
  --tokens 50 \
  --prompt "Mixture-of-Experts enables scaling parameter capacity across distributed home clusters by"

The coordinator connects over TCP, verifies the hardware state, assigns layer boundaries, and streams tokens directly to the console.

Embedding Distributed Inference in C# Code

If you prefer building applications directly in .NET rather than invoking a CLI tool, the coordinator can be embedded using a simple async streaming API: 

using Glacier.Inference.Distributed;

var endpoints = new[]
{
    new StageEndpoint("192.168.1.108", 5055, "RTX 3060 Node"),
    new StageEndpoint("192.168.1.101", 5056, "APU Node"),
    new StageEndpoint("192.168.1.200", 5057, "AVX-512 Server")
};

using var coordinator = new DistributedPipelineCoordinator(
    stages: endpoints,
    modelPath: "models/Mixtral-8x22B-Instruct-v0.1.i1-IQ2_XXS.gguf");

await foreach (var token in coordinator.GenerateStreamAsync("Explain distributed tensor pipelines in simple terms."))
{
    Console.Write(token);
}

Real-World Physical Cluster Benchmarks

Running empirical tests across 4 physical machines over a basic 1 Gbps switch with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B yielded these verified metrics:

  • Prompt Prefill Speed: 52.46 tok/s (6.19x faster than baseline via batched SIMD FMA).
  • Speculative Decode Speed: 23.24 tok/s with 2-stage asynchronous pipeline overlap.
  • Wire Latency: 0.45 ms per LAN hop using fused 64-byte binary framing.
  • Wire Precision: Compressed from 20.4 KB (FP32) to 5,124 bytes (INT8) per token without activation drift.
  • Memory Pressure: 0 collections across Gen0/Gen1/Gen2, guaranteeing zero GC stutter on the hot path.

Repurposing What You Already Own

Large AI models don't have to be restricted to cloud APIs or ultra-high-end enterprise workstations. By pairing lean, zero-allocation network framing with modern SIMD and graphics APIs, you can pool whatever spare hardware you already have sitting on your local network to run models that would otherwise never fit on a single desk machine.

summary: 针对消费级硬件显存（VRAM）不足以运行超大模型（如 Qwen2-57B 或 Mixtral-8x22B）的问题，作者推出了 Glacier.Inference.Distributed。该工具利用流水线并行（Pipeline Parallelism）将 GGUF 的模型层切分到多个计算节点上。通过标准千兆以太网传输激活张量（Activation Tensor）而非模型权重，有效消除了网络延迟成为瓶颈的顾虑。该项目采用纯 C# .NET 10 开发，不依赖 Python 或 C++ 运行时，并实现了零垃圾回收分配，确保推理过程的流畅性。

mainPoints.explanation: 通过将模型层顺序切分到不同配置的设备（如笔记本、台式机、迷你 PC 和服务器），跨越了单机显存容量的物理瓶颈。
在序列解码阶段，节点间仅交换激活张量（KB 级）而非权重，在千兆网下单跳延迟约 0.45ms，占总执行时间不足 0.2%。
基于纯 C# .NET 10 构建，无需复杂的 Python 或 C++ 环境配置，并在热路径循环中实现零内存堆分配，避免 GC 导致的卡顿。

keyQuotes: 将那些不匹配的异构硬件通过标准千兆网络连接成单一流水线集群会怎样？

大型 AI 模型不应局限于云端 API 或超高端的企业级工作站。
